fixtures.rationale: The empty catch block discards the error entirely; the caller has no way to know save(x) failed.
Logging and rethrowing the same error adds a side effect without changing what the caller receives, and is the canonical catch-log-rethrow anti-pattern.
Returning null on failure makes a lookup error indistinguishable from a normal not-found result.
Returning an empty array on failure hides the fact that the orders could not be loaded at all, making it look like there are simply none.
Returning false on failure makes a broken eligibility check indistinguishable from a genuine ineligible result.
validate records the failure against the specific item and returns it, so validateAll can keep processing the rest of the batch instead of stopping on the first bad item.
This is an Express route handler, the entry point where an unhandled failure has to become an HTTP response; turning the error into a 500 is its job, not a swallow.
main is the process entry point; logging the error and setting a nonzero exit code is how a failure surfaces here, since there is no further caller to propagate to.

The handler translates a generic gateway error into a richer, domain-specific PaymentDeclinedError and rethrows it with the original as cause, so the failure still propagates with more information rather than being hidden.

A bare try/finally with no catch clause has no catch to swallow anything in: the parser (oxc, verified directly) reports zero document.errorHandlers for this shape, since ErrorHandlerTarget models catch clauses, not finally blocks. The error still propagates unchanged; the collector produces no candidate at all rather than a cleanup_only one.

loadConfig is a middle layer, not an entry point, and falling back to defaultConfig on any failure hides a real problem (the file is missing, unreadable, or invalid JSON) behind what looks like ordinary default behavior.
The filename matches the default test file pattern, so the rule produces no candidates at all regardless of its contents.
